title: Mock Exam 2
instructions: Closed book, closed notes, no electronic devices. You have 70 minutes. Read every question fully before answering. Write all work you want graded on the FRONT of the page; the backs of pages are scrap and will not be graded. Provide only the number of examples/items a question asks for. For Big-O answers, give the tightest bound you know and justify it (a correct but loose bound earns no credit); say average case vs. worst case wherever it matters (especially for hashing). Use the TEXTBOOK (Weiss) version of every algorithm; a different but valid variant is graded as incorrect. Heaps use the textbook array layout (index 0 unused, root at index 1, children of i at 2i and 2i+1) unless a question says otherwise. Partitioning uses the textbook Section 7.7.2 Hoare method: swap the pivot with the last element, i starts at left and j at right-1, both i and j stop on elements equal to the pivot, and when they cross a[i] is swapped with the pivot. Array indices are 0-based unless stated. Code is C++11 or later using the standard library containers and algorithms; you are never asked to write a sorting algorithm yourself. Point values are shown next to each question.

questions.prompt:
**Question 1 (hash table trace, 12 points)**

A hash table uses **double hashing** with TableSize = 13, hash(x) = x mod 13 and hash2(x) = 7 - (x mod 7), so the i-th probe is (hash(x) + i * hash2(x)) mod 13. Deletion is **lazy** (the cell is marked DELETED, as in the textbook). As in the textbook's findPos, a search or an insertion passes over a DELETED cell that holds a different key and continues probing; a new key is placed in the first EMPTY cell its probe sequence reaches (DELETED cells are not reused). Do not rehash.

Start with an empty table and perform, in order:

insert 18, insert 41, insert 22, insert 44, insert 59, insert 32, insert 31, **remove 18**, find 31, insert 70

a) **(6 points)** Show the table after the seven insertions. For every key that collides, show hash2(x) and the cells probed.

b) **(2 points)** After remove 18, which cells does find 31 examine, in order, and what does it return?

c) **(2 points)** Where does 70 end up? Show hash2(70) and the cells probed, then draw the final table.

d) **(2 points)** Why would hash2(x) = x mod 7 be a bad choice? Why does the textbook want the table size to be prime?

```text
find 31: probed 5, 9, 0 -> found
```

**a)** After the seven inserts: 0:31, 2:41, 5:18, 6:32, 7:59, 9:22, 10:44. (44: home 5 taken by 18, hash2 = 7 - 2 = 5, next cell 5 + 5 = 10. 31: home 5 taken, hash2 = 7 - 3 = 4; cell 9 taken by 22; cell 13 mod 13 = 0 is free.)

questions.prompt:
**Question 2 (heap trace, 10 points)**

Apply the textbook **buildHeap** (min-heap) to the following array stored in the textbook layout (index 0 unused, positions 1 through 12):

`14  7  11  3  9  16  2  12  5  10  8  1`

a) **(7 points)** State the index at which buildHeap's loop starts and ends, then show the array (indices 1-12) after each call to percolateDown.

b) **(1 point)** Why does the loop not start at index 12?

c) **(2 points)** buildHeap makes about n/2 calls to percolateDown, each of which can cost O(log n), yet buildHeap is O(n). Explain why in a few sentences.
questions.answer:
Engine-verified:

```text
buildHeap (min-heap)
  [0]=- | 14 7 11 3 9 16 2 12 5 10 8 1           # start (size 12); percolateDown from i = 6 down to 1
  [0]=- | 14 7 11 3 9 1 2 12 5 10 8 16           # after percolateDown(6) (value 16)
  [0]=- | 14 7 11 3 8 1 2 12 5 10 9 16           # after percolateDown(5) (value 9)
  [0]=- | 14 7 11 3 8 1 2 12 5 10 9 16           # after percolateDown(4) (value 3)
  [0]=- | 14 7 1 3 8 11 2 12 5 10 9 16           # after percolateDown(3) (value 11)
  [0]=- | 14 3 1 5 8 11 2 12 7 10 9 16           # after percolateDown(2) (value 7)
  [0]=- | 1 3 2 5 8 11 14 12 7 10 9 16           # after percolateDown(1) (value 14)
final heap (from index 1): 1,3,2,5,8,11,14,12,7,10,9,16
```
**a)** The loop runs from i = n/2 = **6** down to **1**. After percolateDown(6): `14 7 11 3 9 1 2 12 5 10 8 16`; (5): `14 7 11 3 8 1 2 12 5 10 9 16`; (4): unchanged (3 is smaller than both children); (3): `14 7 1 3 8 11 2 12 5 10 9 16`; (2): `14 3 1 5 8 11 2 12 7 10 9 16`; (1): **1 3 2 5 8 11 14 12 7 10 9 16**.

**b)** Nodes n/2 + 1 through n are leaves; they have no children, so they are already heaps of size 1.

**c)** percolateDown(i) costs time proportional to the **height of node i**, not log n. In a complete tree about n/2 nodes have height 0, n/4 have height 1, n/8 height 2, and so on. The total work is at most the sum of all node heights = n * (1/4 + 2/8 + 3/16 + ...) < n, so buildHeap is **O(n)**. (n separate inserts would cost O(n log n) in the worst case.)
rubric: (1) loop starts at i = n/2 = 6 and runs down to i = 1
(1) after percolateDown(6): 14 7 11 3 9 1 2 12 5 10 8 16
(1) after percolateDown(5): 14 7 11 3 8 1 2 12 5 10 9 16
(1) after percolateDown(4): unchanged (3 is smaller than its children)
(1) after percolateDown(3): 14 7 1 3 8 11 2 12 5 10 9 16
(1) after percolateDown(2): 14 3 1 5 8 11 2 12 7 10 9 16
(1) indices past n/2 are leaves, already heaps
(1) percolateDown cost is proportional to the node's height, and most nodes are near the bottom
(1) sum of heights is bounded by n, so O(n)

**Question 4 (partition trace, 10 points)**

A quicksort call on the subarray below (indices 0 through 10) has been told to use the element at **index 2** as its pivot (a randomly chosen pivot). Use the textbook Hoare partition (7.7.2).

`12  7  10  3  15  9  10  1  14  6  11`

a) **(7 points)** Show the array after the pivot is swapped to the end, after every swap of a[i] and a[j] (say where i and j stopped), and after the pivot is placed in its final position. Give the pivot's final index.

b) **(3 points)** Notice that the array contains a second 10. Why do the textbook's i and j both stop on elements equal to the pivot even though this causes extra swaps? What would happen to quicksort on an array in which every element is equal if they did not stop?

```text
    [6 7 11 3 15 9 10 1 14 12 10]
i stops at index 2, j stops at index 7: swap 11 and 1
    [6 7 1 3 15 9 10 11 14 12 10]
i stops at index 4, j stops at index 6: swap 15 and 10
    [6 7 1 3 10 9 15 11 14 12 10]

    [6 7 1 3 10 9 15 11 14 12 10]

    [6 7 1 3 10 9 10 11 14 12 15]

```
**a)** Pivot value a[2] = 10 is swapped with a[10]: `12 7 11 3 15 9 10 1 14 6 10`. i stops at 0 (12), j stops at 9 (6): swap -> `6 7 11 3 15 9 10 1 14 12 10`. i stops at 2 (11), j at 7 (1): swap -> `6 7 1 3 15 9 10 11 14 12 10`. i stops at 4 (15), j at 6 (**10, equal to the pivot, so j stops**): swap -> `6 7 1 3 10 9 15 11 14 12 10`. Then i stops at 6 (15) and j at 5 (9): crossed, no swap. Swap a[6] with the pivot: **6 7 1 3 10 9 10 11 14 12 15**, pivot index **6**.

**b)** Stopping on equal keys costs a few extra swaps, but it keeps the two parts balanced when there are many duplicates. If every element equals the pivot, i and j each stop at every element, swap, and meet in the **middle**, so the partitions are about equal and quicksort is O(n log n). If they skipped over equal keys, i would run all the way to the end, every partition would be of size n-1 and 0, and quicksort would degrade to **O(n^2)** on an all-equal array.

questions.prompt:
**Question 5 (general knowledge, 2 points each, 10 points)**

Answer each part briefly (about two sentences each).

a) **(2 points)** What is the minimum number of comparisons that **any** comparison-based algorithm needs in the worst case to sort 5 distinct elements? Give the argument (decision tree) and the number.

b) **(2 points)** A quicksort always uses the first element as its pivot. What is its running time on an array that is already sorted, and why?

c) **(2 points)** What is **introsort**? Which three algorithms does it combine, when does it switch between them, and what is its worst-case running time?

d) **(2 points)** State the textbook guarantee for quadratic probing and the two conditions it needs. Why do the first few probe positions have to be distinct?

e) **(2 points)** Why can't a probing hash table delete a key by simply setting its cell back to EMPTY? What does the textbook do instead?
questions.answer:
**a)** A comparison sort is a binary decision tree whose leaves are the possible orderings; there are 5! = 120 leaves. A binary tree with 120 leaves has height at least ceil(log2 120) = **7**, and the worst case needs as many comparisons as the height. (In general Omega(n log n).)

**b)** **O(n^2)**. The first element of a sorted array is the minimum, so every partition splits into sizes 0 and n-1: T(n) = T(n-1) + cn = O(n^2).

**c)** Introsort starts as **quicksort**; if the recursion depth exceeds about 2 log n it switches to **heapsort** for that part; when a subarray gets below a small size threshold it uses **insertion sort**. The depth limit keeps the quicksort part at O(n log n) and the heapsort part is O(n log n), and the insertion sorts total O(n), so the worst case is **O(n log n)**. This is what `std::sort` typically does.

**d)** Theorem 5.1: if the table size is **prime** and the table is **at most half full**, a new element can always be inserted. The proof shows that the first TableSize/2 probe positions are all distinct (if two were equal, (i - j)(i + j) would be divisible by the prime, impossible for small i, j), so at least one of them is empty because at most half of the cells are used.

**e)** If the cell is set to EMPTY, a later search for a key that had been placed after probing *past* this cell would stop at the empty cell and wrongly report "not found" (the probe chain is broken). The textbook uses **lazy deletion**: the cell is marked DELETED; searches continue past it, and it still counts as occupied for the rehash threshold.
rubric: (1) decision tree / 5! = 120 leaves
(1) height >= ceil(log2 120) = 7 comparisons
(1) first-element pivot on sorted input: O(n^2)
(1) reason: partitions of sizes 0 and n-1 (T(n) = T(n-1) + cn)
(1) introsort = quicksort, then heapsort when depth exceeds about 2 log n, insertion sort for small subarrays
(1) worst case O(n log n)
(1) prime table size and at most half full guarantee insertion succeeds
(1) first TableSize/2 probe positions are distinct, so an empty cell must be among them
(1) clearing the cell breaks probe chains: later searches stop early and fail wrongly
(1) lazy deletion: mark DELETED, searches continue past it

questions.prompt:
**Question 6 (design and analyze, 15 points)**

A print server receives **n** print jobs, each with a unique integer ID and an integer priority (larger = more urgent; ties may print in any order). Before any printing starts it also receives **c** cancellation requests, each naming the ID of one job (a job is cancelled at most once; c <= n). When all requests are in, the server prints the ID of every job that was not cancelled, in decreasing order of priority.

To be most efficient as measured by algorithmic time complexity, what data structure(s) will you use and why? Describe your design (name the STL containers and operations) and **fully analyze its complexity** in terms of n and c, stating average versus worst case where it matters. Then answer briefly: (i) can any algorithm that prints the surviving jobs in priority order beat your bound? (ii) if cancellations could instead arrive **while** jobs are already being printed, what small change keeps your design efficient?
questions.answer:
**Design.**
1. Read the c cancellation IDs into an `unordered_set<int> cancelled` (hash set): c inserts, O(1) average each = **O(c)** average. A hash set is the right tool because the only question we ask later is "is this ID cancelled?", and that is O(1) average (a `set` would cost O(log c) per question).
2. Put the n jobs into a `priority_queue<pair<int,int>>` of (priority, ID), a max-heap. Building it from a vector (range constructor / `make_heap`) is **O(n)**; n individual `push` calls would be O(n log n) in the worst case. We need "give me the highest-priority job" repeatedly, which is exactly `top()` + `pop()`.
3. Repeat n times: look at `top()` (O(1)), `pop()` (**O(log n)**), and print the ID only if `cancelled.count(id) == 0` (O(1) average).

**Analysis.** The three steps run one after another, so add them: O(c) + O(n) + n * (O(log n) + O(1)) = **O(n log n + c) = O(n log n)** average (c <= n). Worst case: if the hash set degenerates, each `count` costs O(c), giving O(n log n + nc + c^2) = O(n^2) (never better than O(n log n)). Space O(n).

(i) No. Printing the survivors in priority order is sorting them; every comparison-based algorithm needs Omega(m log m) comparisons for m items (decision-tree bound), and m can be n/2, so O(n log n) is optimal for comparison-based methods. (Equivalent design: erase cancelled jobs from an `unordered_map`, copy the survivors into a vector and sort it: also O(n log n + c).)

(ii) Use **lazy deletion**: do not try to remove a job from the middle of the `priority_queue` (it has no search or erase; that would be O(n)). Just add the ID to the `cancelled` set (O(1)) and, when a job reaches the top, pop and discard it if its ID is in the set. Each job is pushed and popped once, so the cost stays O(log n) per job.
rubric: (3) cancellations kept in a hash set (unordered_set) with O(1) average insert/membership, justified over set/vector
(3) jobs in a priority_queue (max-heap on priority), justified by the repeated 'get highest priority' operation (an alternative such as erase + sort is accepted if analyzed)
(2) the processing loop is described: pop the top, print the ID only if it is not in the cancelled set
(3) complexity: O(c) + O(n) (or O(n log n)) build + n pops at O(log n) = O(n log n + c), steps added
(1) states average vs worst case for the hashing part
(2) (i) comparison-sort lower bound Omega(n log n) for ordering the survivors, so the bound cannot be beaten
(1) (ii) lazy deletion: check the cancelled set when a job reaches the top; the priority_queue cannot erase from the middle
